Executive Legal and Policy Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives

Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program constitutes the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial research and innovation, delivering tax relief to more than 22,000 claimant enterprises annually, including roughly 4,000 businesses operating within the province of Quebec alone. Codified within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA") and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "ITR"), the program is jointly administered through a bifurcated institutional model in which the Department of Finance Canada establishes the legislative policy and statutory framework, while the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) executes technical eligibility assessments and financial compliance audits.

Structurally, the federal SR&ED regime operates through a dual-mechanism incentive design that separates the timing of income tax deductions from the generation of investment tax credits. The first mechanism is the SR&ED Deductible Expenditure Pool governed by section 37 of the ITA. Pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may pool allowable current SR&ED expenditures—and, following legislative restoration effective after December 15, 2024, eligible capital SR&ED expenditures—incurred in Canada. The claimant may deduct the entirety or any portion of this pool in the taxation year incurred to reduce net income for tax purposes, or carry unused pool balances forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in subsequent taxation years. The second mechanism is the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) governed by sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA. Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, claimants earn a volume-based ITC calculated as a statutory percentage of their qualified SR&ED expenditures. Depending on the taxpayer's corporate status, prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, or gross revenue, the ITC is calculated at either an enhanced rate of 35% or a basic rate of 15%, and may be refunded in cash under section 127.1 or applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian federal SR&ED architecture underwent its most significant structural overhaul since the 2012–2014 federal budget reductions. Following a two-phase public consultation process conducted by the Department of Finance between January 31, 2024, and May 27, 2024, alongside an initial funding commitment of $600 million over four years ($150 million per year ongoing) announced in Budget 2024 on April 16, 2024, the federal government unveiled sweeping structural reforms in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) on December 16, 2024. These reforms were subsequently expanded in Budget 2025 and enacted into law via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026.

While the December 2024 FES initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% credit from $3 million to $4.5 million, Bill C-15 legislated a further expansion to $6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, the enacted reforms raised the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historical $10 million–$50 million corridor to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an alternative revenue-based phase-out methodology, extended access to the enhanced 35% refundable credit to eligible Canadian public corporations (ECPCs), restored the SR&ED eligibility of capital expenditures and capital equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, and instituted a voluntary pre-claim approval process launched by the CRA on April 1, 2026.

body.text: The structural consequence of these legislative amendments is a deliberate shift in Canadian fiscal strategy toward mid-market domestic scale-ups and capital-intensive hardware, clean technology, and artificial intelligence (AI) developers. Under the pre-2024 statutory rules, Canadian technology enterprises that completed public listings on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) or Cboe Canada immediately forfeited their Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) status, plunging their SR&ED benefit from a 35% refundable cash credit to a 15% non-refundable tax offset at the precise stage when capital requirements intensified. Similarly, the 2014 elimination of capital expenditure eligibility had penalized domestic manufacturing, robotics, semiconductor, and sovereign AI hardware developers relative to pure software firms. By simultaneously expanding the expenditure cap to $6 million, extending the 35% refundable tier to public corporations, and bringing capital equipment back into scope, Parliament realigned the statutory architecture to prevent premature foreign acquisition of Canadian intellectual property and incentivize domestic industrial scaling.
Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Judicial Precedents
Subsection 248(1) Statutory Pillars and Excluded Activities

The legal gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set forth in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Constructed in general alignment with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Frascati Manual, subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". To qualify under this statutory mandate, the investigation must fall into one of three substantive categories of scientific or technological endeavour, or constitute commensurate support work directly linked to those endeavours.

Under paragraph (a) of the definition in subsection 248(1), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph (b), applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph (c), experimental development encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In administrative practice, the vast majority of industrial SR&ED claims filed in Canada are evaluated under the experimental development branch. Finally, paragraph (d) brings into scope work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Support work under paragraph (d) never qualifies in isolation; its eligibility is strictly derivative. Computer programming, mathematical modelling, or engineering design qualifies only to the extent that the volume and technical scope of that work are strictly necessary—or "commensurate with the needs"—to execute the experiments or analyses required to resolve the underlying scientific or technological uncertainty.

Conversely, subsection 248(1) expressly excludes specific commercial, routine, and non-scientific activities from the definition of SR&ED, even where such activities involve highly skilled technical personnel or occur within a broader innovation project. Statutorily excluded activities encompass market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities (noting that psychological research is eligible under paragraph (d) solely when directly supporting natural science or engineering SR&ED); prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.
Foundational Jurisprudence and the Five-Criteria Legal Test

While subsection 248(1) provides the statutory text, the substantive legal threshold for what constitutes a valid "systematic investigation," "technological uncertainty," and "technological advancement" is governed by binding jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA). The foundational authority in Canadian SR&ED law is Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), 98 DTC 1839. In Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Donald Bowman articulated a rigorous five-criteria test to determine whether a taxpayer's activities satisfy subsection 248(1). The Federal Court of Appeal subsequently affirmed and elevated Justice Bowman's analytical framework as the binding national legal standard in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 8876 (FCA), 99 DTC 5087, and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740.

In its administrative guidance—specifically the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors—the CRA consolidates the five judicial criteria of Northwest Hydraulic into a three-question operational review framework addressed directly in Part 2 (Lines 242, 244, and 246) of Form T661, supplemented by contemporaneous evidentiary verification.

The first judicial criterion asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Justice Bowman held that if the resolution of a problem is reasonably predictable using established engineering methodologies, standard reference manuals, or routine professional competence, no technological uncertainty exists. Technological uncertainty arises either when it is uncertain whether a given objective can be achieved at all, or when system-level constraints—such as conflicting latency, throughput, thermodynamic, or structural parameters—render the path to achieving the objective unpredictable based on publicly available scientific or technological knowledge.

The second judicial criterion asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. This requires a structured five-stage cognitive and operational sequence comprising observation of the subject matter, identification of the specific technological uncertainty, formulation of a testable causal hypothesis explaining how a proposed variable manipulation or architectural design will resolve the uncertainty, methodical testing of the hypothesis through experiment or analysis, and logical evaluation of the results to confirm, modify, or reject the hypothesis.

The third judicial criterion evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. This requirement distinguishes systematic experimental investigation from unguided trial-and-error or ad hoc debugging, mandating that each iterative cycle be informed by the analytical conclusions of the preceding test.

The fourth judicial criterion asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. A technological advancement represents an increase in the stock of technology-base knowledge available to a competent professional in the field, clarifying why a system behaves as it does under specific boundary conditions. Crucially, commercial or technical failure does not disqualify a project; proving through rigorous experimentation that a plausible scientific hypothesis is false eliminates a technological dead-end and constitutes a valid technological advancement under Canadian law.

The fifth judicial criterion asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and the results, was kept as the work progressed. As the Federal Court of Appeal emphasized in RIS-Christie, repeatability is the hallmark of scientific research, making contemporaneous documentation essential to establishing that systematic experimentation actually occurred. Subsequent jurisprudence has sharpened the boundaries of these five criteria across specific industrial and software contexts, creating critical audit traps for unverified claims.

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), 98 DTC 1839
Foundational legal test for SR&ED under s. 248(1) of the ITA across physical modelling of hydraulic structures.

Established the five-criteria test: (1) Technological uncertainty beyond routine engineering; (2) Specific hypotheses; (3) Scientific method discipline; (4) Technological advancement; (5) Contemporaneous records.
Serves as the primary legal benchmark cited by CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) and Tax Court judges in all technical eligibility disputes.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 8876 (FCA), 99 DTC 5087
Evidentiary threshold for Question 5 (contemporaneous documentation) and repeatability of experiments.

Held that while the ITA does not strictly bar oral evidence, repeatability is the hallmark of scientific research; without contemporaneous documentary evidence generated during the work, a claimant will almost invariably fail to prove systematic experimentation.
Retroactive reconstruction of technical narratives at year-end without dated experimental logs, test data, or commit histories risks complete claim denial on audit.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740
Appellate confirmation of the Northwest Hydraulic five-criteria framework.
Confirmed that all five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic represent binding principles of statutory interpretation for subsection 248(1) across all courts in Canada.
Foreclosed arguments that small businesses should be held to a relaxed standard of scientific methodology.
Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, 2007 DTC 41
Distinction between commercial product novelty and technological advancement.

Held by Justice Little that creating a new commercial product or combining known components in a novel functional arrangement does not constitute a technological advancement unless an underlying technological uncertainty was resolved.
Product feature roadmaps and business functional specifications must be separated from underlying engineering or algorithmic bottlenecks.
Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 137
Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) development; "knowledge gap" vs. "technological gap"; oral testimony limits.

Justice Bocock distinguished a subjective "knowledge gap" (where the developer lacks familiarity with a technique that is publicly known) from an objective "technological gap" (where public technology lacks a known solution), and rejected uncorroborated oral testimony.
Software and AI claimants must conduct and document a prior-art / literature review demonstrating why standard documentation, SDKs, or APIs could not resolve the constraint.
Application of the scientific method to food-product formulation and shop-floor development trials.

Chief Justice Rossiter allowed the appeals for the 2013 to 2016 taxation years, holding that Canafric formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at achieving its development goals and rejecting the CRA's characterization of the work as trial-and-error, because Canafric analyzed why unsuccessful recipes failed and modified them accordingly.

Shop-floor, manufacturing, and food-science claimants can satisfy the scientific-method criterion by documenting the analysis of each failed trial run and the resulting modification to the formulation or process.

body.text: The jurisprudential trajectory from Northwest Hydraulic and RIS-Christie through Zeuter Development, Highweb & Page Group, and Canafric demonstrates that technical eligibility in Canada is fundamentally an evidentiary discipline rather than a retrospective technical writing exercise. As Justice Bocock established in Highweb & Page Group, when a claimant fails to document the state of publicly available baseline technology prior to commencing development, the CRA and the Tax Court will recharacterize the engineering effort as overcoming an internal "knowledge gap" involving self-education and routine integration rather than bridging an objective "technological gap". Consequently, embedding hypothesis tracking, baseline benchmarks, and quantitative failure logs directly into daily engineering workflows—such as issue-tracking tickets, version-control pull requests, and laboratory notebooks—is an indispensable prerequisite to surviving a CRA Research and Technology Advisor review.
Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, and Phase-Out Mechanics
Enhanced 35% Refundable Credit and the $6 Million Expenditure Limit

Under subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA, qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and—for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024—Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) are entitled to earn an enhanced Investment Tax Credit of 35% on their qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3) on March 26, 2026, the baseline annual expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA was increased from the historical $3,000,000 cap (and the interim $4,500,000 cap initially proposed in the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement) to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. For a qualifying CCPC or ECPC entitled to the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the maximum annual enhanced SR&ED ITC is computed as:
Maximum Enhanced ITC = $6,000,000 × 35% = $2,100,000

Under section 127.1 of the ITA, the refundability of this enhanced 35% ITC depends on whether the underlying qualified expenditure is of a current or capital nature. For current SR&ED expenditures within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the unused enhanced 35% ITC is 100% refundable in cash for qualifying CCPCs (other than excluded corporations) and ECPCs, providing up to $2,100,000 in direct cash liquidity even when the corporation has zero federal income tax payable. For eligible capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in respect of depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, the unused enhanced 35% ITC earned within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is 40% refundable in cash for a qualifying CCPC, yielding an effective immediate cash refund of 14% (35% × 40%) of the eligible capital cost, with the remaining 21% credit available to offset Part I tax payable or be carried over.
Taxable Capital and Revenue Phase-Out Formulas

The $6,000,000 baseline expenditure limit is not static; it must be shared across all associated corporations pursuant to subsection 127(10.3) of the ITA (filed via Schedule 49, Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) and is subject to a statutory phase-out designed to target the enhanced 35% refundable credit toward small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and mid-market scale-ups.

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out thresholds—calculated on an associated-group basis under Part I.3 of the ITA—were raised from the historical $10,000,000–$50,000,000 range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000. Where the associated group's taxable capital employed in Canada in the immediately preceding taxation year is $15,000,000 or less, the corporation retains the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Where prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada falls between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced linearly at a rate of $1 of expenditure limit lost for every $10 of taxable capital above $15,000,000. Once prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches or exceeds $75,000,000, the enhanced expenditure limit is completely eliminated, and the corporation may claim only the basic 15% non-refundable ITC. Mathematically, under the post-December 15, 2024 rules, the subsection 127(10.2) expenditure limit (EL) under the taxable-capital method for a taxation year of D days is expressed as:
where TCprior represents the aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year.

To accommodate Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—as well as CCPCs that carry substantial balance-sheet debt or equity capital from venture financings—the post-2024 reforms introduced a revenue-based phase-out structure. Under this mechanism, ECPCs have their $6,000,000 expenditure limit reduced as a function of their average gross revenue over the preceding years, and CCPCs are granted the statutory option to elect to use the revenue-based phase-out formula in lieu of the taxable capital phase-out formula. This election serves as a vital tax-planning instrument for capital-intensive biotechnology, clean-technology, or hardware startups that have raised more than $15 million in preferred share or convertible debt capital—which inflates Part I.3 taxable capital employed in Canada—while remaining pre-revenue or low-revenue.
Basic 15% Credit, Refundability Tiers, and Carry-Over Provisions

Qualified SR&ED expenditures that do not qualify for the 35% enhanced rate—including expenditures incurred by large corporations with prior-year taxable capital of $75,000,000 or more, foreign-controlled corporations, non-eligible public corporations, or expenditures of a qualifying CCPC or ECPC that exceed its $6,000,000 expenditure limit—earn the basic federal ITC rate of 15%.

body.text: Unused non-refundable federal SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years to recover Part I corporate income tax paid in prior periods, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset future Part I tax liabilities.

A critical statutory mechanism that must be accounted for in multi-year corporate financial modelling is the taxability of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits. Under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed by a taxpayer in a taxation year—whether utilized to offset Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund under section 127.1—reduces the taxpayer's section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year. If that reduction causes the section 37 pool balance to become negative at the end of the following taxation year, the negative balance must be included directly in the taxpayer's taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA, producing a one-year deferral before the federal ITC becomes subject to corporate income tax. By contrast, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and direct government grants (such as National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program contributions) constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d), meaning they reduce both the section 37 pool and qualified SR&ED expenditures in the same taxation year in which they are received, receivable, or reasonably expected to be received.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Calculation Methodologies
Salaries, Wages, Specified Employees, and Foreign Work Caps

Salaries and wages typically represent the largest component of a Canadian SR&ED claim, governed by subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the ITA and section 2900 of the ITR. To qualify, salary and wages must be incurred in respect of employees who are "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED. Under CRA administrative policy, whether an employee is directly engaged in SR&ED is determined strictly by the hands-on technical tasks performed rather than the employee's corporate title or academic credentials. Eligible directly engaged tasks encompass preparing equipment and materials for experiments, tests, and analyses; carrying out hands-on experimentation, coding experimental algorithms, building physical or digital prototypes, and running analytical simulations; recording measurements, interpreting experimental data, and modifying hypotheses; and providing direct first-line technical supervision of employees performing hands-on SR&ED, where the supervisor possesses technical expertise and directs the ongoing technical course of the experiments, excluding higher-level executive or administrative management.

Three strict statutory restrictions govern the inclusion of salaries and wages in an SR&ED claim. First, under subsections 37(8) and 37(9) of the ITA and subsections 2900(7) through 2900(9) of the ITR, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7 of the ITA (such as employee stock option benefits, company car allowances, or group term life insurance benefits) are excluded from the proxy salary base, and for specified employees, bonuses and profit-based remuneration are completely disallowed as SR&ED expenditures under both calculation methods. Furthermore, pursuant to subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any accrued salary or wages remaining unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in the year until the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid.

Second, the ITA and ITR impose stringent caps on "specified employees," defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as employees who are specified shareholders of the corporation—owning, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any other corporation that is related to the corporation—or who do not deal at arm's length with the employer. For specified employees, the statutory regime enforces two distinct ceilings that must not be conflated. For direct SR&ED salary inclusion (Line 305 of Form T661), subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA caps the maximum directly engaged SR&ED salary claimable for a specified employee at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year during which the individual was a specified employee. Separately, for the purpose of calculating the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for overhead under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the ITR, the amount of a specified employee's salary that may enter the proxy salary base is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary and wages for the year (excluding bonuses and taxable benefits) and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year. Mathematically, the proxy salary base inclusion (Sproxy, spec) for a specified employee is governed by:
Sproxy, spec = min( SSR&ED, 0.75 × Stotal, 2.5 × YMPE × Demployed ÷ 365 )

Third, while SR&ED must generally be carried on within Canada, subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA permits a claimant to include salaries and wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada, subject to a hard statutory cap of 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages paid to employees directly engaged in SR&ED carried on in Canada. To qualify for this 10% foreign carve-out, three cumulative conditions must be satisfied: the employee performing the work outside Canada must be a resident of Canada; the work performed outside Canada must be solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer; and the remuneration must not be subject to an income or profits tax imposed by the foreign country in which the work was performed. Payments to foreign subcontractors or non-resident employees working outside Canada are completely ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives.
Proxy Method Versus Traditional Overhead Method

A taxpayer claiming SR&ED must elect annually on Line 160 of Form T661 whether to calculate overhead and other expenditures using the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA, this election must be made on the first Form T661 filed for the taxation year and is statutorily irrevocable for that taxation year once filed.

A frequent error in secondary commentary is the assertion that the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is 65% of direct salaries. In point of law, 65% has not been the statutory rate since December 31, 2012; the rate transitioned to 60% for the 2013 calendar year and was permanently set at 55% effective January 1, 2014. Pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Prescribed Proxy Amount is strictly 55% of the SR&ED salary base.

body.text: The strategic divergence between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method has become acutely consequential for Canadian artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and data analytics companies. In conventional software engineering, human labour accounts for the vast majority of R&D expenditure, making the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount overwhelmingly advantageous. Conversely, when an AI enterprise trains custom foundation models or neural networks on proprietary datasets, its expenditures on elastic cloud GPU compute and data processing frequently approach or surpass total engineering payroll. If such an AI company reflexively elects the Proxy Method on Line 160 of Form T661, it is legally barred from claiming any of its cloud computing invoices, because under Regulation 2900 the 55% PPA stands in lieu of all overhead and other expenditures. Only by electing the Traditional Method can the claimant itemize and claim dedicated cloud computing and data processing expenses directly as incremental SR&ED overhead on Line 360, unlocking substantial incremental tax credits whenever actual eligible overhead exceeds 0.55 times the capped SR&ED salary base.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures (depreciable property) and expenditures for the right to use property (equipment leases) were completely excluded from both the section 37 SR&ED deduction pool and the section 127 ITC calculation. Following the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, Budget 2025, and the enactment of Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), Parliament restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and lease costs effective for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024) and lease amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024.

Under the restored rules codified in Form T661 (Lines 390, 400, 535, 540, and 558), an expenditure qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure if it is incurred to acquire new or used depreciable property that becomes available for use after December 15, 2024, and is intended to satisfy either of two "All or Substantially All" (ASA) statutory tests. Under the operating time test, the claimant must intend to use the depreciable property all or substantially all—defined administratively by the CRA as 90% or more—of its operating time throughout its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada. Alternatively, under the value consumption test, the claimant must intend to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of the property's value in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, which frequently applies to specialized pilot-plant rigs, custom test benches, or experimental tooling and moulds acquired after December 15, 2024.

Strict statutory boundaries and transitional rules govern this capital restoration. Depreciable property acquired before December 16, 2024, and lease costs incurred before December 16, 2024, do not qualify for SR&ED tax incentives under any circumstances. If a claimant's taxation year straddles December 16, 2024 (having begun before December 16, 2024), the claimant must calculate SR&ED operating use as a percentage of total operating time strictly for the period after December 15, 2024. Furthermore, land is a non-depreciable capital asset and never qualifies for SR&ED, while buildings and leasehold interests in buildings remain statutorily excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures. If the claimant elects the Proxy Method, lease costs for general purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) are similarly excluded.

For equipment used partially for SR&ED and partially for commercial operations, the SR&ED ITC calculation for Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) applies identically under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, although the capital cost of SUE does not enter the section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and must instead be depreciated under the regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8. Additionally, under the Traditional Method, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of its operating time may be claimed on a prorated basis on Line 360 of Form T661 as overhead and other expenditures.

Where technology assets do not meet the 90% ASA SR&ED threshold, or where a taxpayer claims standard tax depreciation, capital recovery is governed by Schedule 8 CCA classes: Class 50 provides a 55% declining-balance rate for general-purpose electronic data processing equipment and systems software, including AI hardware; Class 46 provides a 30% declining-balance rate for data network infrastructure equipment; Class 44 provides a 25% declining-balance rate for patents or rights to use patented information; Class 12 provides a 100% rate for application software and perpetual software licences, subject to the half-year rule; and Class 8 provides a 20% declining-balance rate for general machinery and peripheral equipment. Crucially, Budget 2024 enacted Temporary Immediate Expensing for Productivity-Enhancing Assets, allowing businesses to immediately write off 100% of the cost of eligible property in Classes 44, 46, and 50 acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and available for use before January 1, 2027.
Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers, Materials, and Third-Party Payments

Beyond direct salaries, overhead, and capital property, four categories of external and material expenditures enter the SR&ED calculation. When a claimant contracts with an arm's-length person or partnership to perform SR&ED on the claimant's behalf in Canada, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is included in the section 37 deductible pool, but pursuant to the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, only 80% of the eligible contract payment is included in qualified SR&ED expenditures for calculating the section 127 Investment Tax Credit. This 20% statutory reduction strips out the assumed commercial profit margin of the subcontractor. To prevent double-claiming, the statement of work and invoices must demonstrate that the subcontractor performed eligible SR&ED work in Canada on the payer's behalf.

In contrast, payments made to a non-arm's-length corporation (such as a parent, subsidiary, or sister corporation) for performing SR&ED do not directly qualify as qualified expenditures in the hands of the payer. Instead, the related party that actually performed the SR&ED incurs the underlying salaries, materials, and capital costs, and the two non-arm's-length parties may execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the qualified expenditures to the payer (reported on Line 540 of Form T661, including post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures on Line 535), alongside Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length). Separately, third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D consortia—where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results in its business even without controlling the day-to-day research—are included at 80% for section 127 ITC purposes.

Finally, under Regulation 2900(2)(a), a claimant may include the cost of materials that are either consumed (rendered virtually valueless or destroyed during experimental runs) or transformed (incorporated into a prototype, pilot plant, or experimental batch) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. If an experimental prototype or transformed material is subsequently sold commercially or converted into a commercial asset, the lesser of the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value) and the original material cost claimed is subject to SR&ED recapture under subsections 127(27) through 127(35) of the ITA, clawing back the previously earned ITC by adding it directly to federal Part I tax otherwise payable.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Every Canadian province (with the exception of Prince Edward Island, which utilizes discretionary innovation rebates) and the Yukon Territory maintains a statutory R&D tax credit or grant-in-tax program that stacks on top of the federal SR&ED regime. Except for Quebec and Alberta, which administer their corporate tax systems independently through Revenu Québec and Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA), provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the CRA via harmonized T2 corporate income tax schedules.

body.text: Detailed Regional Nuances and Structural Divergences
Ontario (Three-Tiered Regime)

Ontario operates three complementary corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario). The primary SME incentive is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on T2 Schedule 566, which provides an 8% refundable tax credit (adjusted from 10% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) to qualifying CCPCs with a permanent establishment in Ontario on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures. Unlike the federal SR&ED expenditure limit—which eliminated its taxable income phase-out in 2019 and now phases out solely on taxable capital ($15M–$75M) or revenue—Ontario's $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit remains subject to a dual phase-out: it begins to phase out when the associated group's prior-year Ontario taxable income exceeds $500,000 (and is eliminated completely at $800,000) or when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $25,000,000 (eliminated at $50,000,000).

Complementing the OITC is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on T2 Schedule 508, which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations (both CCPCs and large or foreign-controlled corporations) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures net of any OITC claimed. Once a profitable CCPC exceeds $800,000 in prior-year taxable income and loses its OITC entitlement, it retains eligibility for the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC. The third tier is the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), which provides a 20% refundable tax credit on up to $20 million of qualified expenditures incurred under an eligible R&D contract with an approved Ontario university, college, or hospital research institute. In addition, interactive software and gaming developers in Ontario frequently segregate eligible development labour into the Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (OIDMTC), which provides a 35% to 40% refundable credit, while hardware manufacturers leverage the Ontario Made Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit (OMMITC), which was enhanced up to 15% refundable in Budget 2025.
Quebec (Revenu Québec Distinct Architecture)

Quebec does not harmonize its R&D tax credit base with the federal Form T661 expenditure pool; instead, corporations file distinct provincial claims directly with Revenu Québec. For fiscal years beginning before March 25, 2025, Quebec maintained eight specialized R&D tax measures anchored by the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D). Under this flagship measure, eligible SMEs earn up to a 30% fully refundable credit on the first $3,000,000 of eligible Quebec R&D salaries, while large corporations (and SME expenditures exceeding $3,000,000) earn a 14% fully refundable credit. Unlike the federal program, Quebec's primary R&D credit applies strictly to R&D salaries and wages (included at 100%) and arm's-length Quebec subcontractors (included at 50%), excluding materials and overhead from the standard salary credit calculation. Furthermore, Quebec imposes a statutory exclusion threshold of $50,000 for SMEs—scaling linearly up to $225,000 for large businesses—of non-creditable baseline R&D salary before the credit begins to accrue.

Quebec historically supplemented the salary credit with 30% SME and 14% large-business refundable credits on 80% of university research contracts, pre-competitive private partnership research (100% of current expenses and 80% of subcontracting contracts), and research consortium dues (100% of contributions), alongside an industrial design credit (24% SME and 12% large on designers' salaries, 50% of subcontracts, and equipment costs), a technology adaptation services credit (40% on 80% of fees paid to a College Centre for the Transfer of Technologies or liaison centre), and a five-year personal income tax holiday for foreign researchers and foreign experts exempting 100% of salary in years one and two, 75% in year three, 50% in year four, and 25% in year five. For fiscal years beginning on or after March 25, 2025, Quebec reformed its innovation tax credit suite to consolidate parallel measures while preserving its core refundable R&D support profile.
Alberta (Innovation Employment Grant — Incremental Model)

Effective January 1, 2021, Alberta replaced its historical 10% flat SR&ED credit with the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), legislated under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and detailed in Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration Information Circular IEG-1. Unlike volume-based credits in other provinces, the Alberta IEG employs a hybrid base-plus-incremental formula on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta R&D spending, which must match expenditures eligible for the federal SR&ED program. The IEG provides an 8% payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's "base level of spending," defined as the mathematical average of the corporation's qualifying Alberta R&D expenditures over the immediately preceding two taxation years, and an enhanced 20% payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures that exceed that two-year rolling average base level.

Because a first-year R&D claimant—or a corporation establishing a new R&D centre in Alberta with zero prior-year Alberta R&D spend—has a two-year historical average base level of $0, 100% of its Year 1 Alberta R&D expenditures exceed the base, earning the full 20% refundable rate (worth up to $800,000 on $4,000,000 of eligible spending). The IEG phases out incrementally for corporations with associated taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 and is completely eliminated at $50,000,000 or above. Claims are filed with Alberta TRA using AT1 Schedule 29 (Form A29) and Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Claimed in Alberta) within 15 months after the corporation's filing due date (21 months after fiscal year-end, affording claimants a three-month window following the 18-month federal SR&ED filing deadline).
Interaction with Direct Grants, Clean Tech ITCs, and Stacking Mechanics

Canadian R&D performers routinely stack federal SR&ED tax credits with provincial R&D credits and direct non-repayable or conditionally repayable government contributions. The primary federal direct funding instruments interacting with SR&ED include the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which provides non-repayable cost-shared financial contributions covering internal technical salaries and contractor costs for SMEs, supplemented by the $100 million NRC AI Assist Program announced in Budget 2024 to help Canadian SMEs build and deploy AI solutions. In the artificial intelligence sector, additional stacking instruments include the $2 billion AI Compute Access Fund and Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy announced in Budget 2024, Scale AI (which reimburses up to 40% of eligible project expenses on approved AI adoption and commercialization projects), and FedDev Ontario's Regional AI Initiative (RAII), which provides interest-free repayable contributions of $125,000 to $5,000,000 covering up to 50% of eligible project costs. In the industrial sustainability sector, the Clean Technology and Clean Technology Manufacturing Investment Tax Credits—enacted and expanded across Budget 2024 and the 2024 Fall Economic Statement—provide up to a 30% refundable ITC on eligible clean technology property and clean technology manufacturing machinery and equipment, including polymetallic mining and the extraction and processing of six critical minerals.
Mathematical Mechanics of Government Assistance "Grinding"

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, any "government assistance" or "non-government assistance" that a taxpayer receives, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED reduces ("grinds") the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar before the federal SR&ED ITC is calculated. Direct government grants (such as NRC IRAP) reduce both the provincial R&D expenditure base and the federal SR&ED expenditure base. Furthermore, provincial R&D tax credits—such as Ontario's 8% OITC, Ontario's 3.5% ORDTC, or Alberta's 8%/20% IEG—constitute "government assistance" for federal tax purposes and therefore reduce the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure base after adding back the Prescribed Proxy Amount when the Proxy Method is elected.

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics, consider a qualifying Ontario CCPC electing the 55% Proxy Method that incurs $100,000 of directly engaged non-specified SR&ED salaries (S = $100,000). Under a pure federal and provincial tax credit stack without direct grants, the unadjusted qualified expenditures (QE0) equal the $100,000 direct salary plus the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount of $55,000, totalling $155,000:
The refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC at 8%) applies to the $155,000 expenditure base, generating $12,400 in refundable provincial credits:
Next, the non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC at 3.5%) is computed on the Ontario eligible expenditure base net of the $12,400 OITC, yielding $4,991:

Assuming the corporation is profitable and does not waive the non-refundable ORDTC, total Ontario government assistance equals $12,400 + $4,991 = $17,391, which grinds the federal qualified expenditure base (QEfed) down to $137,609:

Applying the enhanced 35% federal SR&ED ITC rate to $137,609 produces a 100% refundable federal credit of $48,163.15, resulting in a combined federal and provincial tax credit recovery of $65,554.15, or 65.55% of the initial $100,000 salary outlay:

If the corporation is in a tax loss position and waives the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC so as not to grind its 35% refundable federal credit, federal qualified expenditures remain $155,000 − $12,400 = $142,600, generating a refundable federal ITC of 35% × $142,600 = $49,910 and a combined pure cash refund of $49,910 + $12,400 = $62,310 (62.31% of direct salary).

The financial leverage expands substantially when the same Ontario CCPC stacks a 50% NRC IRAP salary contribution (G = $50,000) onto the $100,000 of direct SR&ED salary while electing the 55% Proxy Method and waiving the non-refundable ORDTC. Under Regulation 2900(4), an NRC IRAP reimbursement reduces the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures on Form T661, but does not reduce the salary base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. Consequently, the corporation still generates the full $55,000 notional proxy overhead on the $100,000 gross SR&ED salary, establishing gross expenditures plus proxy of $155,000. Deducting the $50,000 NRC IRAP grant leaves net eligible expenditures of $105,000. The 8% Ontario OITC on $105,000 yields $8,400 in refundable provincial cash, which further reduces federal qualified expenditures to $105,000 − $8,400 = $96,600. The 35% federal enhanced SR&ED ITC on $96,600 generates $33,810 in refundable federal cash, bringing total non-dilutive cash recovery across NRC IRAP ($50,000), Ontario OITC ($8,400), and federal SR&ED ($33,810) to $92,210, or 92.21% of the direct R&D salary expenditure:

Because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under Regulation 2900(4) is calculated on gross eligible SR&ED salary before deducting NRC IRAP salary assistance, stacking an NRC IRAP contribution with federal and provincial SR&ED credits under the Proxy Method enables a qualifying CCPC to recover over 92 cents on the dollar in non-dilutive cash. Conversely, with respect to the 30% refundable Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC and restored SR&ED capital expenditures, the ITA prohibits claiming two federal Investment Tax Credits on the same capital property cost; consequently, taxpayers acquiring dual-purpose clean-tech pilot equipment after December 15, 2024, must compare the 30% Clean Tech Manufacturing ITC (which is 100% refundable) against the 35% enhanced SR&ED ITC on capital property (which is 40% refundable in cash, yielding a 14% immediate cash refund plus a 21% non-refundable credit).
Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, Audit Defence, and Statutory Penalties
Statutory Forms and the Absolute 18-Month Reporting Deadline

To claim federal SR&ED tax incentives, a taxpayer must file prescribed technical and financial forms alongside its income tax return. Every claimant must submit Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), which captures project-by-project technical narratives (Part 2, Lines 242, 244, and 246), project cost breakdowns, expenditure pool calculations (Part 3), qualified expenditure and PPA calculations (Part 4), statistical data, and mandatory claim preparer disclosures (Part 9). Concurrently, corporate claimants must file Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations)—while unincorporated individuals file Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit – Individuals)—to compute the section 127 ITC, claim the section 127.1 refund, or carry credits back or forward.

The statutory reporting deadline for SR&ED is governed by subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Under these provisions, Form T661 and Schedule 31 (or Form T2038(IND)) must be filed on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing due date for the taxation year. For a corporation, the T2 income tax return filing due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA is 6 months after the end of its taxation year; adding the 12-month SR&ED reporting period establishes a strict statutory deadline of 18 months after the end of the corporation's taxation year.

Pursuant to subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA, the Minister of National Revenue has no statutory authority or administrative discretion to extend the 18-month SR&ED filing deadline. If a claimant submits Form T661, Schedule 31, or omitted prescribed line items even one day after the 18-month statutory bar, the expenditures are permanently and irrevocably barred from qualifying as SR&ED expenditures, with no discretionary relief available before the CRA or the Tax Court of Canada.
Voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

To increase upfront fiscal certainty and reduce post-filing audit friction, the CRA launched a formal, voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026. Canadian-controlled private corporations, other Canadian corporations, and Canadian partnerships are eligible to apply provided that they have annual gross income of less than $25,000,000 and are in good standing with the CRA. Through this mechanism, CRA Research and Technology Advisors evaluate the technical eligibility of planned R&D projects before work begins or costs are incurred, providing binding upfront assurance on whether the projects satisfy the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED; an approval is valid for up to three years, and the CRA aims to complete the expenditure review of claims containing pre-approved projects within 90 days rather than 180 days.
Claim Preparer Penalties and Expanded CRA Audit Powers

Parliament has paired the 2024–2026 expansion of SR&ED benefits with stringent statutory penalties and expanded audit enforcement authorities. Part 9 of Form T661 requires complete disclosure of whether a third-party claim preparer assisted in preparing the claim, the preparer's business number, and the exact billing arrangement, including whether the advisor was compensated on a contingency basis or fixed fee. If required claim preparer information is missing, incomplete, or false on Form T661, subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA imposes a strict $1,000 penalty per SR&ED claim, for which the claimant corporation and the external claim preparer are jointly and severally liable.

Furthermore, under the tax administration amendments introduced in Budget 2024, the CRA received three potent statutory enforcement tools applicable to corporate and SR&ED audits. First, the CRA is authorized to issue a formal "Notice of Non-Compliance" to a taxpayer that fails to comply with a requirement or notice to provide documentation or assistance during an audit, which carries an automatic monetary penalty while the notice remains outstanding. Second, the CRA is empowered to require that any oral or written information, responses, or project documentation during an audit be provided under oath or solemn affirmation. Third, Budget 2024 expanded the statutory "stop-the-clock" rules, suspending the normal reassessment limitation period whenever a taxpayer challenges a CRA requirement for information or receives a Notice of Non-Compliance.
Strategic Conclusions and Compliance Recommendations for Canadian Innovators

The post-Bill C-15 Canadian R&D tax incentive landscape offers one of the most generous non-dilutive capital recovery regimes in the OECD—capable of returning $2,100,000 annually in federal refundable credits alongside provincial credits and grants—yet simultaneously demands rigorous statutory and evidentiary compliance. To capture the full benefit of the reformed regime while insulating claims against CRA technical and financial reassessment, corporate taxpayers and their tax advisers should institutionalize four structural compliance protocols.

First, finance teams at artificial intelligence, machine learning, and simulation-heavy enterprises must systematically re-evaluate their annual overhead methodology election rather than defaulting to the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under Regulation 2900(4). Because cloud computing, GPU cluster hosting, and software subscriptions are statutorily absorbed within the 55% notional proxy rate and cannot be claimed separately under the Proxy Method, compute-intensive claimants whose dedicated cloud and post-December 15, 2024 partial-use equipment lease costs exceed 55% of their capped SR&ED salary base should elect the Traditional Method on Line 160 of Form T661 to capture actual incremental infrastructure overhead on Line 360.

Second, hardware, robotics, clean-technology, and advanced manufacturing enterprises acquiring laboratory instruments, pilot rigs, or dedicated AI server clusters on or after December 16, 2024, must implement contemporaneous equipment utilization logs demonstrating that the depreciable property is used 90% or more (All or Substantially All) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada. Where newly acquired capital property is also potentially eligible for the 30% refundable Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC or the Budget 2024 Temporary Immediate Expensing measure for Classes 44, 46, and 50, tax controllers should model the comparative cash-flow and refundability yields prior to allocating the asset across T2 schedules.

Third, emerging technology companies with "specified employees" (founders holding 10% or more of any class of shares) must structure founder compensation through regular T4 base salary rather than dividends or performance bonuses, as dividends and bonuses earn zero SR&ED tax credits and proxy salary base inclusions are strictly capped at 75% of base salary and 2.5 times the YMPE under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the ITR. Concurrently, venture-backed CCPCs whose Part I.3 taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds the $15,000,000 phase-out threshold due to preferred equity or debt financings should evaluate electing the revenue-based phase-out structure introduced in the 2024–2026 reforms to preserve their full $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit.

Fourth, in light of the evidentiary standards established in RIS-Christie, Highweb & Page Group, and Canafric—combined with the CRA's Budget 2024 statutory authority to compel audit responses under oath or affirmation—claimants must eliminate retrospective year-end narrative reconstruction. Engineering teams must document baseline prior-art limitations at the outset of each project to establish an objective "technological gap" rather than an internal "knowledge gap," formulate explicit causal hypotheses before executing test runs, and archive dated quantitative results within their version-control and project-management repositories. Finally, eligible businesses with annual gross income below $25,000,000 should utilize the CRA's voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process launched on April 1, 2026, to secure binding technical eligibility determinations before starting planned projects.
